title: What is Free Cash Flow?
subtitle: OCF − CapEx = the cash a business is genuinely free to use
openingQuestion: FCF = OCF − CapEx. Why is CapEx subtracted?
openingOptions: Because CapEx is real cash spent to maintain and grow the asset base - money no longer free
explanation: Free cash flow is what's left after a business has spent enough to maintain and expand its operating capacity - operating cash flow minus asset investment. This is the number that decides whether a business truly sustains itself, because only from here comes the cash to pay debt, pay dividends, or buy back stock without having to borrow more. It's also the figure sitting in the numerator of every discounted-cash-flow model.

diagram.label: What's left is free cash flow
Used to pay debt, pay dividends, buy back shares, or acquire companies

realWorldExample.description: FPT has stable Operating Cash Flow from its technology and telecom segments, while CapEx stays at a moderate level relative to revenue (mostly investing in data-centre infrastructure and R&D). As a result, FPT's Free Cash Flow is usually reliably positive - the foundation letting the company pay an annual cash dividend while still continuing to invest in expanding its digital-transformation business abroad.

quiz.question: Buffett calls FCF 'owner earnings'. What does that mean?
options: The cash left on the balance sheet at the end of the period
All the accounting profit the company generated during the period
The cash shareholders genuinely benefit from after sustaining the business
Operating cash flow before subtracting investment spending
quiz.explanation: Buffett defines owner earnings as Net Income + D&A − maintenance CapEx. This is the cash truly generated for the owner. FCF is the foundation of DCF valuation.

quiz.question: Why do many value investors see Free Cash Flow (FCF) as a more reliable metric than Net Income for valuing a business?
options: Because FCF is separately confirmed by auditors each period
Because FCF is always larger than accounting profit in every industry
Because FCF is unaffected by any accounting policy choice
Because FCF is real cash left after sustaining the asset base
quiz.explanation: Net Income is shaped by many accounting choices and estimates (depreciation, provisions, revenue recognition) that can differ between companies with similar underlying businesses. FCF, based on real cash flow, is much harder to adjust at will - which is why Warren Buffett prioritises 'owner earnings' (close to FCF) over Net Income when valuing a company.

quiz.question: A company has OCF of 500 billion and CapEx of 350 billion. What is its Free Cash Flow?
options: 150 billion, the cash left over after investing to sustain the business
850 billion, since CapEx is an investment and should be added to cash flow
500 billion, since CapEx belongs to investing and isn't subtracted from FCF
350 billion, exactly equal to what the company spent investing during the period
quiz.explanation: FCF = OCF − CapEx = 500 − 350 = 150 billion. This is the amount the company is genuinely free to use: paying debt, dividends, buybacks, or acquiring another company.

quiz.question: Why do value investors prioritise FCF over accounting profit?
options: Because FCF is always larger than accounting profit, so it reflects better financial health
Because FCF also subtracts the cash needed to sustain the business, while profit doesn't
Because FCF is independently audited while profit is self-calculated by the company
Because accounting profit is only ever disclosed once a year, at year-end
quiz.explanation: Profit subtracts depreciation - an estimate - but doesn't subtract actual CapEx. A company that has to spend 400 billion every year just to keep its production capacity intact doesn't really own that portion of profit for its shareholders.

quiz.question: A company has negative FCF for two years running. When is that acceptable?
options: Never acceptable - negative FCF is always a sign of impending bankruptcy
Always fully acceptable, since negative FCF just simply means the company is investing very heavily
When the CapEx is for expansion and there's evidence the investment is generating a return
When the company still pays a steady dividend funded with money borrowed from a bank
quiz.explanation: Negative FCF from building a plant about to come online is entirely different from negative FCF from constantly pumping in cash just to keep revenue flat. The question is always: will this CapEx eventually turn back into cash flow, and when.

quiz.question: Why does Buffett call FCF 'owner earnings'?
options: Because this figure is calculated separately for each shareholder based on their ownership stake
Because only the company's owner is allowed to see this number in the reports
Because it equals exactly the dividend the company has committed to pay shareholders
Because it's the amount an owner can withdraw without harming the business
quiz.explanation: If you owned the entire company, FCF is the amount you could genuinely take home this year while the company still runs unimpaired next year. Accounting profit can't answer that question.

keyTakeaways: FCF is the cash a business is genuinely free to use after sustaining itself
FCF underlies DCF valuation and Buffett's 'owner earnings'

practicePrompt.question: A company has OCF (Operating Cash Flow) of 500 billion for the year, and spends 350 billion maintaining and upgrading its production plant (CapEx). What is this company's Free Cash Flow (FCF), and what does that number mean?
options: FCF = 500 billion, exactly equal to OCF, since CapEx doesn't affect the company's free cash flow
FCF = 500 - 350 = 150 billion, the cash that is genuinely free once the business has been kept running
FCF = 850 billion, adding OCF and CapEx together since both are positive cash flows for the company
FCF cannot be calculated without knowing the company's Net Income for the period
practicePrompt.explanation: FCF = OCF − CapEx = 500 - 350 = 150 billion. This is the cash genuinely free after sustaining the business (unlike OCF, which hasn't yet subtracted the investment needed to sustain the asset base) - the foundation of DCF valuation and Warren Buffett's concept of 'owner earnings'.

application.title: Calculate FCF yourself
application.message: Take the latest cash flow statement of a listed company you're interested in, find the 'cash from operating activities' and 'fixed-asset purchases' lines, and subtract to get FCF yourself.
application.secondary: If OCF is positive but FCF is negative, the company is investing heavily - not necessarily a bad sign.

sections.text: If you had to pick a single number to judge a business's financial health, many legendary investors - including Warren Buffett - would pick Free Cash Flow (FCF), not Net Income.
A simple but powerful formula: FCF = OCF − CapEx

Free Cash Flow is calculated as Operating Cash Flow minus CapEx (capital expenditure). The logic is intuitive: OCF is the cash a business generates from its operations, but part of that must be reinvested into fixed assets to sustain and grow production capacity - that's CapEx. What's left after subtracting CapEx is truly 'free' - the company has full discretion over what to do with it: pay debt, pay dividends, buy back shares, do M&A, or simply build up a cash reserve.

This is why FCF is considered a more honest measure than Net Income: Net Income can be distorted by non-cash accounting entries (D&A, early revenue recognition), while FCF reflects the real cash a business generates after subtracting the investment it's required to make just to keep operating.

Warren Buffett uses a similar concept called 'owner earnings': Net Income + D&A − maintenance CapEx (excluding growth CapEx). He argues this is the number that truly reflects the value a business creates for shareholders each year, and it's the foundation for valuing a business through the Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) method.

items: Large positive FCF: a business has many options - paying debt, dividends, buybacks, M&A
Negative FCF at a growth company: acceptable if the expansion CapEx is reasonable
FCF is the core input for DCF valuation models

concepts.def: OCF minus CapEx - cash a business has full discretion over after sustaining operations.
Warren Buffett's concept: NI + D&A − maintenance CapEx, measuring real value created for shareholders.
A valuation method based on the present value of future FCF.

sections.label: Negative FCF isn't always bad
sections.text: A fast-growing company (like many tech startups or retail chains expanding rapidly) can show negative FCF for years because growth CapEx exceeds OCF - as long as that investment genuinely produces a proportionate return in future revenue and profit.

lines: FCF = OCF − CapEx is one of the most important formulas in corporate finance.
